Expectation1: Listen actively and provide emotional support when needed.
Situation1: Your friend calls you in the middle of the night, crying, because they just received some devastating family news.
Expectation2: Stay updated on changes in laws and legal precedents.
Situation2: An attorney in a case before you has just cited a new appellate court decision from last week that could be relevant. You need to review it before the next session.
Story: It was 1:30 a.m. when my phone buzzed, jolting me from the dense legal text I’d been poring over. On the other end, my friend’s voice trembled, barely coherent through sobs. She’d just learned her father was in critical condition, and she needed someone—needed me—to listen, to be present, to help her hold together the pieces of her world. I wanted nothing more than to give her my full attention, to offer the comfort she deserved. But the appellate court decision the attorney cited earlier that day was still open on my laptop, its implications gnawing at my mind. Tomorrow’s session would demand my complete understanding of this new precedent, and I knew the attorneys would expect me to be fully prepared. My heart ached for my friend, but the weight of my judicial responsibility pressed down just as heavily. I sat there, phone in hand, torn between the urgent needs of someone I cared about and the unyielding demands of the bench.
